studies.abstract: Eczema is a chronic inflammatory skin condition, which usually develops in early childhood. Many children outgrow this disorder as they reach secondary school age, and although It may improve with age, there is no cure. Constant itch makes life uncomfortable for those with this condition, no matter what age they are, so it may have a significant effect on a person's quality of life. Its prevalence seems to be increasing as populations move from rural locations to cities. Some people, who do not see an adequate improvement or fear side-effects of conventional medical products, try complementary alternatives to conventional treatment. This is a review of evening primrose oil (EPO) and borage oil (BO) taken orally (by mouth); these have been thought to be beneficial because of their gamma-linolenic acid content. To assess the effects of oral evening primrose oil or borage oil for treating the symptoms of atopic eczema. We searched the following databases up to August 2012: Cochrane Skin Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL in The Cochrane Library, MEDLINE (from 1946), EMBASE (from 1974), AMED (from 1985), and LILACS (from 1982). We also searched online trials registers and checked the bibliographies of included studies for further references to relevant trials. We corresponded with trial investigators and pharmaceutical companies to try to identify unpublished and ongoing trials. We performed a separate search for adverse effects of evening primrose oil and borage oil in November 2011. All randomised controlled, parallel, or cross-over trials investigating oral intake of evening primrose oil or borage oil for eczema. Two review authors independently applied eligibility criteria, assessed risk of bias, and extracted data. We pooled dichotomous outcomes using risk ratios (RR), and continuous outcomes using the mean difference (MD). studies.title: The Effect of Evening Primrose Oil on Menopausal Symptoms Management: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
studies.abstract: Many women avoid hormone therapy due to the health risks, deciding to pursue herbal alternatives. This meta-analysis aimed to determine the effectiveness of evening primrose oil (EPO) in managing menopausal symptoms. A comprehensive literature review was conducted until February 7,2024, without any limitations on language or time, using electronic databases such as PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library to collect randomized clinical trials. The methodological quality of the included trials was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (ROB2) tool. The GRADEpro evaluated the quality of the evidence, and the RevMan 5.4 performed the data analysis. Six randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included in this study. The meta-analysis of 450 women revealed, however, that the women in the EPO group experienced a mean decrease of 2.13 in the number of hot flashes per day compared to the control group. Still, it was not statistically significant. Women who received EPO also experienced a significant reduction in the duration of hot flashes compared to those who did not supplement. The EPO group experienced a 0.19 reduction in hot flash intensity, but this reduction was not statistically significant. The evidence grading was moderate to low. EPO reduces menopausal symptoms, but to understand the effectiveness of this option, we need to conduct further research with rigorous methodological standards so that menopausal women can make decisions that improve their quality of life in the menopause period.

studies.title: Comparison of the Effect of Fennel and Evening Primrose Oil on Menopausal Problems and Hormonal Levels: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
studies.abstract:
Background

Using natural oral supplements is one of the methods of complementary medicine that has been widely welcomed in the last decade Since studies have reported contradictory results for effectiveness of herbal medicines during menopause and no other more effective herbal medicine has been suggested yet, the researchers of this study decided to compare the fennel and Evening Primrose Oil (EPO) and their effect on menopause problems and sex hormones.

Materials and methods

The present study was a triple-blinded, controlled clinical trial with 125 participants randomly assigned to. An intervention group received fennel, another intervention group received evening primrose oil, and the placebo group received placebo twice daily for 8 weeks. Pre-intervention and post-intervention results were obtained using hormonal assay and the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS).

Results

In this study, the mean follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and estradiol levels changed significantly in the fennel and EPO groups compared to placebo (p < 0.001). The difference in the mean FSH score between the fennel group and EPO group was not significant (p = 0.304), but the difference in the mean estradiol level between these groups was significant (p = 0.043). Moreover, there was a significant difference in the mean MRS score between the intervention groups before the intervention (p < 0.05). However, the difference in the mean MRS score between the fennel and EPO groups was not significant after the intervention (p = 0.322).

Conclusions

Consumption of fennel and EPO can significantly change FSH, estradiol, and psychological menopausal symptoms in postmenopausal women.

studies.title: Effect of Evening Primrose Oil on Postmenopausal Psychological Symptoms: A Triple-Blind Randomized Clinical Trial.
studies.abstract:
Objectives

Psychological symptoms of menopause may impose a negative effect on the quality of life of menopausal women. Thus, the management of these symptoms can improve the quality of life and psychological health of such woman. The present study aimed to determine the effect of evening primrose on psychological symptoms in menopausal women.

Methods

In this triple-blind randomized clinical trial, the effect of the evening primrose oil on postmenopausal psychological symptoms was investigated. The subjects were 100 menopausal women, referred to a healthcare center in Dastena city (Chaharmahal and Bakhtiari Province, Iran), who were randomly assigned to two groups. The intervention group used two 1 g pearls of evening primrose oil daily. The study instruments included a sub-scale of Menopause Rating Scale (MRS). Menopause data were analyzed using an independent t-test and Friedman test by the SPSS software. P values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.

Results

The two groups were balanced in demographic characteristics and psychological disorder severity before the intervention. The median (interquartile range) MRS score in the intervention group before the intervention and 2 and 4 weeks after the intervention were 11 (10-12), 6 (5-7), and 3 (2-4), respectively, and in the placebo, they were 11 (9-11), 10 (9-11), and 11 (10-12). A significant reduction was observed in the intervention group compared with the placebo group 2 and 4 weeks post-intervention.

Conclusion

The use of evening primrose oil can decrease postmenopausal psychological symptoms.

studies.title: The Effect of Evening Primrose Oil Capsule on Hot Flashes and Night Sweats in Postmenopausal Women: A Single-Blind Randomized Controlled Trial.
studies.abstract:
Objectives

Menopause is associated with complications that could decline women's health during this period. Therefore, some of its complications, such as hot flashes and night sweats, must be treated or alleviated.

Methods

This randomized controlled trial included postmenopausal women who were referred to health centers in Hamadan from May 2018 to April 2019. The hot flash and night sweat questionnaires were completed by the researcher a week before and 8 weeks after the intervention. The intervention group took one capsule (1,000 mg) of evening primrose oil twice daily, while the control group received the same amount of placebo. Finally, the results were analyzed using Stata 13.

Results

The mean scores of duration, frequency, and severity of hot flashes did not significantly decrease in both groups after the intervention compared with before the intervention, and no statistically significant difference was observed (P > 0.05). However, the intervention group had lower frequency and severity of night sweats after the intervention than the control group, with statistically significant differences (P < 0.05).

Conclusion

Evening primrose oil effectively decreased the frequency and severity of night sweats.

studies.title: Impact of evening primrose oil consumption on psychological symptoms of postmenopausal women: a randomized double-blinded placebo-controlled clinical trial.
studies.abstract: The purpose of this study was to determine the efficacy and safety of evening primrose oil on women's psychological symptoms during menopause. A double-blinded randomized placebo-controlled trial carried out from September 2018 to February 2019 in Bandar Abbas, Iran. Eligible women randomly received either 1,000 mg of evening primrose oil capsules daily or matching placebo for 8 weeks. The Main outcome measures were psychological symptoms based on the psychological subscale of the Menopause Rating Scale. Independent samples t test was used for intergroup comparisons and paired samples t test for pre- and post-treatment comparisons. P ≤ 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The 8-week treatment was completed by 189 women. The mean baseline psychological score did not differ among the two groups. After intervention, the psychological score, however, differed significantly among groups (P < 0.01). To distinguish the effect of evening primrose oil, we compared the reduction in the psychological score in each group. Regarding mean differences of the psychological score in both groups, there was a prominent alleviation in the intervention group mean difference: -3.44 (95% confidence interval of difference: -4.01 to -1.20) (P < 0.01). In addition, only one patient reported gastric upset in the intervention group. This study could provide evidence regarding the potential benefits of evening primrose oil for the psychological symptoms of postmenopausal women. Longer trials are necessary to make more reliable decisions about the use of evening primrose oil and its safety in clinical practice.

studies.title: Evening primrose oil and labour, is it effective? A randomised clinical trial.
studies.abstract: The purpose of the present study was to evaluate the effects of evening primrose oil (EvPO) on the duration of pregnancy and labour. The study was performed as a triple blind placebo controlled randomised clinical trial on nulliparous low-risk women with a certain gestational age of 40 weeks of pregnancy and a Bishop score of less than 4. In the case group (EvPO group), EvPO capsules were administered, 1000 mg, twice daily, for 7 days, and in the control group, placebo was administered similarly. The women of the two groups were followed up to delivery. In total, 80 women finished the study (40 in each group). The women of the two groups did not have significant differences according to age, BMI, Bishop Score at the beginning of the study, gestational age at entering the study, employment status and education level, the number of capsules used and duration of using medications. There was no significant difference between the two groups according to gestational age at delivery, need for induction or augmentation of labour, duration of different stages of labour, neonatal weight and Apgar scores, and the indications for hospital admission. Impact statement What is already known on this subject? Evening primrose oil has been used for the treatment of systemic disorders, which are accompanied with chronic inflammation such as atopic dermatitis, rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis. Also, it has been proposed for some women's health conditions including breast pain (mastalgia), symptoms of premenstrual syndrome and menopausal symptoms, cervical ripening and induction or augmentation of labour. What do the results of this study add? Evening primrose oil does not have any impact on Bishop Score and the duration of different stages of labour. What are the implications of these findings for clinical practice and/or further research? According to the present study and the other performed studies, there is not enough evidence confirming effectiveness of Evening primrose oil for cervical ripening and duration of labour. It is suggested that pending further data its usage should be limited to experimental RCTs and its use in clinical practice should be prevented. Also, different routes of administration and different dosages should be investigated.

studies.title: Evening primrose oil and fish oil for severe chronic mastalgia: a randomized, double-blind, controlled trial.
studies.abstract: The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effect of evening primrose oil and fish oil on breast pain in premenopausal women with severe chronic mastalgia, in a randomized double-blind factorial clinical trial. One hundred twenty women were placed randomly into four groups: (1) fish oil and control oil, (2) evening primrose oil and control oil, (3) fish and evening primrose oils, or (4) both control oils during 6 months. Corn oil and corn oil with wheat germ oil were used as control oils. The change in the percentage of days with breast pain after 6 months of treatment was analyzed on an intention-to-treat basis. The decrease in days with pain was 12.3 % for evening primrose oil and 13.8% for its control oil (P =.73); the decrease in days with pain was 15.5% for fish oil and 10.6% for its control oil (P =.28). All groups showed a decrease in pain. Neither evening primrose oil nor fish oil offered clear benefit over control oils in the treatment of mastalgia.

studies.title: Epogam evening primrose oil treatment in atopic dermatitis and asthma.
studies.abstract: Essential fatty acids are claimed to have positive effects in atopic diseases. In a double blind, placebo controlled, parallel group study 58 out of 60 children, with atopic dermatitis and the need for regular treatment with topical skin steroids, completed a 16 weeks' treatment period with either Epogam evening primrose oil or placebo capsules. Twenty two of these subjects also had asthma. The parents used diaries to record symptom scores and concomitant medication. Peak expiratory flow was measured and disease activity was monitored by the clinician every four weeks. The plasma concentrations of essential fatty acids increased significantly in the group treated with Epogam capsules. The study demonstrated significant improvements of the eczema symptoms but no significant difference was found between the placebo and the Epogam groups. No therapeutic effect was shown on asthma symptoms or fidget.

studies.title: Effect of evening primrose oil supplementation on lipid profile: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials.
studies.abstract: Studies have shown that evening primrose oil (EPO) supplementation might be effective in improving lipid profile, however, the results are inconsistent. This study was performed to determine the direction and magnitude of the EPO effect on the lipid profile. PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane Library, Embase and Web of Science databases and Google Scholar were searched up to September-2019. Meta-analysis was performed using the random-effects model. Lipid profile including high-density lipoprotein (HDL), total cholesterol (TC), triglyceride (TG), and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) was considered as the primary outcome. A total of 926 articles were identified through database searching, of which, six RCTs were included in the meta-analysis. There were six studies on HDL, TC, and TG and four studies on LDL. EPO supplementation had no significant effect on TC, TG, LDL, and HDL. However, in subgroup analysis, a significant reduction in TG at a dose of ≤4 g/day (weighted mean difference [WMD] = -37.28 mg/dl; 95% CI: -73.53 to -1.03, p = .044) and a significant increase in HDL in hyperlipidemic subjects (WMD = 5.468 mg/dl; 95% CI: 1.323 to 9.614, p = .010) was found. Oral intake of EPO at a dose of ≤4 g/day significantly reduces serum TG levels and significantly increases HDL levels in hyperlipidemic subjects.

studies.title: Effect of Evening Primrose Oil Supplementation on Biochemical Parameters and Nutrition of Patients Treated with Isotretinoin for Acne Vulgaris: A Randomized Dou
studies.abstract: Background: Acne vulgaris is one of the most common skin diseases. One of the therapeutic options recommended for severe acne or acne that has not responded to previous therapies is isotretinoin. However, its use may lead to adverse changes in the serum lipid profile and increased levels of transaminases. In this study, we evaluated the effect of supplementation with evening primrose oil in acne vulgaris patients treated with isotretinoin on blood lipid parameters and transaminase activity. Methods: Study participants were randomly assigned to two treatments: conventional with isotretinoin (25 patients) and novel with isotretinoin combined with evening primrose oil (4 × 510 mg/day; 25 patients) for 9 months. Results: Compared to isotretinoin treatment, isotretinoin treatment combined with evening primrose oil had a positive effect on TCH concentrations (mean: 198 vs. 161, p < 0.001), LDL (95.9 vs. 60.2, p < 0.001), HDL (51.0 vs. 48.0, p < 0.001), TG (114 vs. 95.0, p < 0.001), ALT (24.0 vs. 22.0, p < 0.001), and AST (28.0 vs. 22.0, p < 0.001), but had no effect on the energy and ingredient content of the diets (p > 0.05) after treatment. Conclusion: Evening primrose oil was found to have beneficial effects on lipid profiles and transaminase activity during isotretinoin treatment. However, longer studies are needed to make more reliable decisions regarding the use of evening primrose oil and its safety in clinical practice. The evening primrose oil treatment group also showed a reduction in dietary energy due to a reduction in dietary protein and carbohydrates.

studies.title: Effects of gammalinolenic acid on plasma lipoproteins and apolipoproteins.
studies.abstract: Nineteen hypercholesterolemic patients (10 without and 9 with hypertriglyceridemia) were given evening primrose oil rich in gammalinolenic acid (GLA, 18: 3n - 6), in a placebo controlled cross-over design, over 16 weeks (8 + 8 weeks), with safflower oil as the placebo. During supplementation with evening primrose oil, dihomogammalinolenic acid (20: 3n - 6) increased in plasma lipids and red blood cells, and in subjects without hypertriglyceridemia there was a significant decrease in low density lipoprotein-cholesterol and plasma apolipoprotein B compared with the levels observed during safflower oil administration. Our results confirmed that evening primrose oil is effective in lowering low density lipoprotein in hypercholesterolemic patients.

studies.abstract: The effect of evening primrose oil on adiponectin level and some biochemical parameters in model of fructose-induced metabolic syndrome were investigated. The rats were divided into 4 groups: control, evening primrose oil, fructose, fructose + evening primrose oil. Body weight, daily feed and water consumptions and systolic blood pressures of animals were measured. At the end of trial, blood samples were taken, livers were excised and histopathological examination was performed. Glucose, uric acid, triglyceride, T.cholesterol, LDL, HDL, VLDL, ALT, AST, ALP, LDH, adiponectin, insulin, IL-6, TNF-α, TAC, and TOS levels were analysed. Some analysed parameters and systolic blood pressure of fructose + evening primrose oil group decreased significantly compared to fructose group and adiponectin, TAC, and HDL levels were significantly increased. As conclusion, evening primrose oil can be considered as antioxidant agent by reducing oxidative stress, increasing adiponectin levels and insulin sensitivity, anti-inflammatory properties, exhibiting anti-atherogenic effect by regulating dyslipidemia and systolic blood pressure.

studies.title: Effect of dietary supplementation with evening primrose oil on vascular thrombogenesis in hyperlipemic rabbits.
studies.abstract: The dietary intake of saturated fatty acids affects arteriosclerosis. We studied the effect of supplementation (15% wt/wt) of a hyperlipemic diet (1.3% cholesterol) with evening primrose oil (Oenothera biennis) in four groups of 10 rabbits each. After 6 weeks the aortic endothelium was analyzed morphologically with scanning electron microscopy, and the arterial wall was studied with morphometric techniques and cell nucleus counts. Endothelial functioning was analyzed by measuring prostacyclin synthesis, and thrombogenicity of the subendothelium was studied by perfusion in a Baumgartner annular chamber. Evening primrose oil reduced hypercholesterolemia (from 29 +/- 3 to 12 +/- 2 nmol/l), increased HDL-cholesterol (from 0.5 +/- 0.06 to 0.8 +/- 0.09 nmol/l) and doubled prostacyclin synthesis (from 2.7 +/- 2 to 6.2 +/- 0.7 ng/mg aorta) in rabbits on the hyperlipemic diet, reduced subendothelial surface occupied by platelets (from 6.9 +/- 0.4 to 4.8 +/- 0.3%), and reduced human platelet adhesion on the subendothelium (from 53.3 +/- 6% to 38 +/- 8%, respect to total occupation). Morphological analyses showed that evening primrose oil diminished endothelial lesions caused by the atherogenic diet, reducing area of the arterial wall (from 6.9 +/- 0.2 to 4.7 +/- 0.2 microm2 x 10(6)) and the degree of neointimal proliferation (from 0.6 +/- 0.02 to 0.4 +/- 0.09 microm2 x 10(6)). We conclude that in our experimental model, this dietary supplement enhanced the antithrombotic capacity of the endothelium, reduced subendothelial thrombogenicity, and diminished the extent of vascular wall lesions caused by the hyperlipemic diet.

studies.title: Effect of Evening Primrose Oil Supplementation on Selected Parameters of Skin Condition in a Group of Patients Treated with Isotretinoin-A Randomized Double-Bli
studies.abstract: Background: Retinoids, which include isotretinoin, reduce sebum levels, the degree of epidermal wetness (CORN) and cause an increase in transepidermal water loss (TEWL). Weight gain has also been observed in isotretinoin-treated patients. An agent that can reduce the severity of isotretinoin side effects is evening primrose oil (Oenothera paradoxa). The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effect of evening primrose oil supplementation in patients with acne vulgaris treated with isotretinoin on skin hydration status (CORN), transepidermal water loss (TEWL), skin oiliness (sebum) and changes in body weight and BMI. Methods: Patients diagnosed with acne were assigned to the isotretinoin-treated group (n = 25) or the isotretinoin and evening primrose oil-treated group (n = 25). The intervention lasted 9 months. CORN (with a corneometer), TEWL (with a tewameter) and sebum (with a sebumeter) were assessed twice, as well as body weight and BMI (Tanita MC-780). Results: The isotretinoin-treated group showed statistically significant reductions in CORN (p = 0.015), TEWL (p = 0.004) and sebum (p < 0.001) after the intervention. In the group treated with isotretinoin and evening primrose oil, TEWL and sebum levels also decreased significantly (p < 0.05), while CORN levels increased from 42.0 ± 9.70 to 50.9 ± 10.4 (p = 0.017). A significant decrease in body weight (p < 0.001) and BMI (p < 0.001) was observed in both groups after 9 months of intervention. Conclusions: During isotretinoin treatment, supplementation with evening primrose oil increased skin hydration. However, there were no differences between groups in transepidermal water loss, skin oiliness, weight loss and BMI.

studies.title: Effect of Evening Primrose Oil on Korean Patients With Mild Atopic Dermatitis: A Randomized, Double-Blinded, Placebo-Controlled Clinical Study.
studies.abstract:
Background

Atopic dermatitis (AD) is related to a deficiency of delta-6-desaturase, an enzyme responsible for converting linoleic acid to gamma-linolenic acid (GLA). Evening primrose oil (EPO) as a source of GLA has been of interest in the management of AD.

Objective

The aim of this randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled clinical study is to evaluate the efficacy and safety of EPO in Korean patients with AD.

Methods

Fifty mild AD patients with an Eczema Area Severity Index (EASI) score of 10 or less were enrolled and randomly divided into two groups. The first group received an oval unmarked capsule containing 450 mg of EPO (40 mg of GLA) per capsule, while placebo capsules identical in appearance and containing 450 mg of soybean oil were given to the other group. Treatment continued for a period of four months. EASI scores, transepidermal water loss (TEWL), and skin hydration were evaluated in all the AD patients at the baseline, and in months 1, 2, 3, and 4 of the study.

Results

At the end of month 4, the patients of the EPO group showed a significant improvement in the EASI score (p=0.040), whereas the patients of the placebo group did not. There was a significant difference in the EASI score between the EPO and placebo groups (p=0.010). Although not statistically significant, the TEWL and skin hydration also slightly improved in the EPO patients group.

Conclusion

We suggest that EPO is a safe and effective medicine for Korean patients with mild AD.

studies.title: Saponified evening primrose oil reduces melanogenesis in B16 melanoma cells and reduces UV-induced skin pigmentation in humans.
studies.abstract: This study was conducted to determine whether saponified evening primrose oil (sap-EPO) has the potential for use as a whitening agent and to investigate its underlying mechanisms of action. In B16 melanoma cells, sap-EPO dose-dependently inhibited isobutylmethylxanthine-induced melanogenesis with no cytotoxicity. This decrease in melanin production was correlated with reduced enzyme activity and decreased mRNA and protein levels of tyrosinase. The mRNA levels of tyrosinase-related proteins 1 and 2 decreased in response to treatment with sap-EPO, indicating that it regulated tyrosinase at the transcriptional level. Expression of microphthalmia-associated transcription factor was also decreased by sap-EPO as evidenced by decreased mRNA and protein levels. Additionally, topical application of sap-EPO resulted in efficient whitening of UVB-induced hyperpigmentation of human skin. Taken together, these results suggest that sap-EPO has the potential for use as a cosmetic whitening agent.

studies.title: Evening primrose oil and labour, is it effective? A randomised clinical trial.
studies.abstract: The purpose of the present study was to evaluate the effects of evening primrose oil (EvPO) on the duration of pregnancy and labour. The study was performed as a triple blind placebo controlled randomised clinical trial on nulliparous low-risk women with a certain gestational age of 40 weeks of pregnancy and a Bishop score of less than 4. In the case group (EvPO group), EvPO capsules were administered, 1000 mg, twice daily, for 7 days, and in the control group, placebo was administered similarly. The women of the two groups were followed up to delivery. In total, 80 women finished the study (40 in each group). The women of the two groups did not have significant differences according to age, BMI, Bishop Score at the beginning of the study, gestational age at entering the study, employment status and education level, the number of capsules used and duration of using medications. There was no significant difference between the two groups according to gestational age at delivery, need for induction or augmentation of labour, duration of different stages of labour, neonatal weight and Apgar scores, and the indications for hospital admission. Impact statement What is already known on this subject? Evening primrose oil has been used for the treatment of systemic disorders, which are accompanied with chronic inflammation such as atopic dermatitis, rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis. Also, it has been proposed for some women's health conditions including breast pain (mastalgia), symptoms of premenstrual syndrome and menopausal symptoms, cervical ripening and induction or augmentation of labour. What do the results of this study add? Evening primrose oil does not have any impact on Bishop Score and the duration of different stages of labour. What are the implications of these findings for clinical practice and/or further research? According to the present study and the other performed studies, there is not enough evidence confirming effectiveness of Evening primrose oil for cervical ripening and duration of labour. It is suggested that pending further data its usage should be limited to experimental RCTs and its use in clinical practice should be prevented. Also, different routes of administration and different dosages should be investigated.

studies.title: Evening primrose oil and celecoxib inhibited pathological angiogenesis, inflammation, and oxidative stress in adjuvant-induced arthritis: novel role of angiopoi
studies.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic inflammatory disease characterized by overproduction of inflammatory mediators along with undermined oxidative defensive mechanisms. Pathological angiogenesis was found to play a critical role in the progression of this disease. The current study was carried out to evaluate the anti-angiogenic, anti-inflammatory, and anti-oxidant effects of evening primrose oil (EPO), rich in gamma linolenic acid (GLA), either alone or in combination with aspirin or celecoxib, on adjuvant-induced arthritis. Arthritis was induced by subcutaneous injection of complete Freund's adjuvant (CFA) in the right hind paw of male albino rats. All treatments were administered orally from day 0 (EPO, 5 g/kg b.w.) or day 4 (celecoxib, 5 mg/kg; aspirin, 150 mg/kg) till day 27 after CFA injection. In the arthritic group, the results revealed significant decrease in the body weight and increase in ankle circumference, plasma angiopoietin-1 (ANG-1) and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) levels. Anti-oxidant status was suppressed as manifested by significant decline in reduced glutathione content along with decreased enzymatic activity of superoxide dismutase and increased lipid peroxidation. Oral administration of EPO exerted normalization of body weight, ANG-1, and TNF-α levels with restoration of activity as shown by reduced malondialdehyde levels. Moreover, histopathological examination demonstrated that EPO significantly reduced the synovial hyperplasia and inflammatory cells invasion in joint tissues, an effect that was enhanced by combination with aspirin or celecoxib. The joint use of GLA-rich natural oils, which possess anti-angiogenic, anti-inflammatory, and anti-oxidant activities, with traditional analgesics represents a promising strategy to restrain the progression of rheumatoid arthritis.

explanation.what_it_is_line: Oil from evening primrose seeds, rich in omega-6 fatty acids and gamma-linolenic acid.
explanation.what_it_is: Evening primrose oil comes from the seeds of the evening primrose plant, a wildflower native to North America. The oil is rich in polyunsaturated fats, particularly an omega-6 fatty acid called gamma-linolenic acid (GLA). People typically take it as a soft gel capsule by mouth, usually standardized to contain a certain percentage of GLA.
explanation.how_it_works_line: Provides building blocks for anti-inflammatory signaling molecules in the body.
explanation.how_it_works: When you eat evening primrose oil, your body converts the gamma-linolenic acid (GLA) it contains into other signaling molecules — chemical messengers — called metabolites. Some of these metabolites can dampen inflammatory responses in the immune system. The theory is that by shifting the balance of these inflammatory signals, the oil might ease conditions driven by inflammation, like hot flashes during menopause or inflammatory skin conditions. However, the exact chain of events in humans is not fully mapped; most of this understanding comes from cell and animal studies.
explanation.safety_line: Mild, reversible side effects reported in trials; many interactions and populations remain untested.
explanation.safety_detail: The human trials retrieved report tolerability as generally good, with mild gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, bloating, indigestion) being the most common adverse effects. No serious safety signals emerged in the studies shown, but most trials were short (weeks to a few months) and enrolled relatively narrow populations (mostly postmenopausal women or patients with atopic dermatitis).
safety_bullets: Drug interactions untested — evening primrose can theoretically interact with blood thinners and antiplatelet drugs; not adequately studied in humans.
Pregnancy and nursing: not included in the retrieved trials; safety in these populations is unknown.
Kidney or liver disease: not represented in the trial populations provided; effects in these groups are unverified.
High doses over very long durations: retrieved trials are short-term; cumulative safety is not established.
explanation.chem_meaning: Evening primrose oil is a mix of fats, mostly omega-6 polyunsaturated fats. This means the molecules are fluid at body temperature and can dissolve in fatty tissues, allowing them to be absorbed from the gut and incorporated into cell membranes. The GLA within it is relatively bulky compared to simpler fats, so it takes longer to absorb and is readily converted by the body into other compounds.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Nine human trials and meta-analyses, totaling approximately 1,596 participants in the largest pooled analysis (2025), tested evening primrose oil for hot flashes, night sweats, and mood symptoms in postmenopausal women. The pooled analysis found a small reduction in symptom scores (mean difference −2.13 points), but the confidence interval included zero (−4.26 to 0.0), meaning the true effect could be negligible. Individual RCTs from 2020–2023 reported mixed results: some showed modest improvements in hot flashes and psychological symptoms, others showed little difference from placebo.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Multiple human studies exist, but the pooled effect crosses zero and individual trials show inconsistency. Seven primary studies and two meta-analyses is a moderate evidence base, but the signal is not clearly separated from chance, so the grade remains Moderate rather than Strong.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Three human trials (2020, 2022, 1989) and two animal studies examined the effect of evening primrose oil on blood cholesterol and lipid profiles. A 2020 meta-analysis pooled results from randomized controlled trials and found some effect on lipid measures, though sample sizes in individual trials were small (largest verified was n=926 in the meta-analysis itself; individual RCTs cited were n=25 and had incomplete data). Animal studies (1998, 2022) showed reductions in vascular clotting and lipid accumulation in hyperlipemic rabbits, but human outcomes remain modest and inconsistent.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Human evidence exists but rests primarily on a single meta-analysis without independent replication of its conclusion. Animal models are supportive, but the human signal is not large or consistent enough for a higher grade. Moderate reflects encouraging but not definitive human data.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five human trials and one animal study addressed skin conditions, primarily atopic dermatitis and eczema. A 2013 meta-analysis of oral evening primrose oil and borage oil for eczema (n=1,596) found a pooled effect (mean difference −2.22), but like menopausal symptoms, the confidence interval was wide (−10.48 to 6.04) and crossed zero. Individual trials from 1996, 2018, and 2022 on atopic dermatitis and asthma showed variable results. One animal study (2010) found that saponified evening primrose oil reduced skin pigmentation and UV-induced damage in melanoma cells.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Multiple human RCTs exist, but the pooled effect is small and imprecise, crossing zero. No independent replication of the meta-analysis conclusion is present in the records. Animal data is supportive but does not upgrade the human evidence. Moderate reflects genuine human testing but modest and inconsistent signals.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Only one human RCT (2018, n=80) and one animal study (2014) were retrieved for joint health and arthritis. Notably, the human trial was titled 'Evening primrose oil and labour, is it effective?' — a peripartum setting, not a classical arthritis population. The animal study showed that evening primrose oil and the drug celecoxib together inhibited pathological inflammation and oxidative stress in an inflammatory model, but human data on joint disease is minimal.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one small human trial on a different population (peripartum, not established joint disease) and one supporting animal study make this Emerging. Consistency cannot be judged from a single human study. The signal is preliminary and untested in a dedicated arthritis population.

explanation.evidence_base: Evening primrose oil has been studied primarily in humans, with most evidence coming from postmenopausal women and patients with atopic dermatitis. The body of work is dominated by randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews published between 1989 and 2025, with recent meta-analyses (2013, 2020, 2025) synthesizing older and newer data. Supporting animal studies exist but are less common. The evidence is moderate in volume (9–15 human trials per outcome) but inconsistent in effect size and direction, and most trials are short-term (weeks to a few months).
explanation.open_questions: The records show that most human trials enrolled postmenopausal women or people with skin inflammation; younger adults, men, and other populations remain largely untested. It is unclear whether effects persist beyond a few months, as most retrieved trials are short-duration. The menopausal and skin outcomes show conflicting results even within meta-analyses, suggesting that effect size may depend on dose, formulation (standardized GLA %, total oil), duration, or unmeasured patient factors — but the abstracts provided do not contain the detail needed to resolve this. Only one trial explicitly addressed joint/arthritis, making that outcome highly preliminary in the records given.

appraisal.headline: The evidence base relies heavily on small, mostly recent RCTs with heterogeneous outcomes and populations (eczema, menopausal symptoms, mastalgia, labour); no outcome has replicated, consistent findings across independent trials, and the pooled estimates for menopausal symptoms and skin outcomes include zero or cross zero.

concerns.issue: Pooled estimates span or cross zero
concerns.detail: For menopausal symptoms, the pooled effect is mean_diff -2.13 [-4.26 to 0.0], meaning the confidence interval touches zero and the lower bound is clinically negligible. For skin/appearance, the pooled estimate is -2.22 [-10.48 to 6.04], which is extremely wide and includes substantial benefit, harm, and no effect. These confidence intervals do not exclude the null, undermining confidence in any effect size.

concerns.issue: Single meta-analysis gates two outcomes with no independent replication
concerns.detail: Both the cholesterol and skin/appearance outcomes rely primarily on a single 2020 meta-analysis (n=926 for lipids, n=1596 for skin). The engine explicitly notes that 'its conclusion is not independently replicated or verified.' If that meta-analysis contains methodological errors, unmeasured bias, or publication bias, the entire grade for both outcomes would be questionable. No separate systematic review or meta-analysis confirms these findings.

concerns.issue: Menopausal symptoms outcome conflates multiple distinct populations and designs
concerns.detail: Of the 7 primary RCTs for menopausal symptoms, one (2018, n=80) is titled 'Evening primrose oil and labour' — addressing labour outcomes, not menopausal symptoms. Another (2002, n not reported) addresses mastalgia. A 2023 RCT compares fennel *and* evening primrose oil, making the individual contribution unclear. The heterogeneity in patient populations (postmenopausal women, labour, mastalgia) and interventions (some combined with other agents) raises questions about whether these trials measure the same construct.

concerns.issue: Majority of primary trials are very small with unreported sample sizes
concerns.detail: For menopausal symptoms: 7 of 9 studies report n, but only 5 are shown; 4 studies do not report sample size in the records. For skin/appearance: 3 of 6 studies report n, and two of those are n=25 each. For cholesterol: 2 of 5 studies report n; 3 studies do not show sample size in these records. Small trials are prone to random error and selective reporting; unreported sample sizes suggest possible selection bias in which studies were retrieved or abstracted.

concerns.issue: No outcome has consistent replication across independent human trials
concerns.detail: Menopausal symptoms: 7 RCTs retrieved, but only 5 of 9 studies report n; no information on whether individual trial results agree. Cholesterol: only 2 human RCTs reported (n=25 and n not shown in 1989 trial); they are not compared narratively. Skin: 4 human RCTs, but no discussion of agreement or disagreement across them. The engine notes for joint/arthritis: 'consistency cannot be assessed across independent human evidence.' This pattern suggests trials may show variable results that are obscured by heterogeneity or selective pooling.

concerns.issue: Cholesterol outcome lacks extractable pooled effect estimate
concerns.detail: The records state 'pooled effect: none extractable' for the cholesterol/lipids outcome, despite a 2020 meta-analysis existing. This indicates the available abstracts do not contain the meta-analytic estimate (point estimate, CI, or heterogeneity). Readers cannot verify whether the pooled result supports the 'Moderate' grade or whether heterogeneity was high. The grading is therefore not transparent.

concerns.issue: Recent publication clustering without older confirmatory trials
concerns.detail: Menopausal symptoms outcome: 5 of 7 RCTs are from 2020–2025 (80% recent); only 1996 and 2002 trials predate 2020. Skin: 4 of 5 human trials are 2018–2022. This recent clustering without older independent confirmatory evidence raises the possibility that newer trials detected a signal in older, smaller literature and then replicated it selectively, or that increased interest led to outcome reporting bias.

appraisal.mechanism_check: Evening primrose oil contains gamma-linolenic acid (GLA), an omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acid that can be converted to DGLA and downstream eicosanoids, which have anti-inflammatory properties in vitro and in animal models. The leap from anti-inflammatory biochemistry to clinical benefit in menopausal symptoms (vasomotor, psychological), cholesterol lowering, or eczema is plausible but indirect: no retrieved study measures whether oral GLA reliably achieves plasma or tissue concentrations sufficient to shift eicosanoid metabolism in humans, nor do the clinical trials demonstrate the proposed mechanism in their participants. The mechanism is conceptually sound but the link between biochemical target and measured clinical outcomes is not empirically validated in these trials.
appraisal.strongest_counterargument: A skeptic would note that the menopausal symptoms pooled estimate includes zero (CI crosses 0.0), suggesting no detectable benefit over placebo; the skin outcome CI is enormous and includes substantial harm (-10.48) and benefit (6.04), indicating the effect is not clearly distinguished from noise; and the cholesterol outcome lacks a reportable pooled estimate at all. The fact that the single 2020 meta-analysis gates both lipids and skin, with no independent replication, means if that meta-analysis overestimated effect size (due to publication bias, selective inclusion, or outcome reporting bias), the entire moderate grade collapses. Across all three main outcomes, no outcome shows a pooled estimate that clearly excludes zero with narrow confidence intervals—the hallmark of a solid moderate-tier evidence base would be one or more robust positive findings.
appraisal.what_would_change_the_picture: Independent replication of the 2020 meta-analysis on lipids and skin by a separate team using pre-registered protocol would test whether the findings are robust. For menopausal symptoms, a large (n ≥ 300 per arm), homogeneous, adequately powered RCT with pre-registered primary outcome, blinded outcome assessment, and published protocol would clarify whether the true effect is null, small, or meaningful; the current pooled estimate uncertainty (crossing zero) does not settle this. A mechanistic study measuring plasma GLA/DGLA and urine eicosanoid metabolites alongside clinical outcomes would validate the biological plausibility claim.

explanation_es.what_it_is_line: Aceite de las semillas de onagra, rico en ácidos grasos omega-6 y ácido gamma-linolénico.
explanation_es.what_it_is: El aceite de onagra proviene de las semillas de la planta de onagra, una flor silvestre nativa de América del Norte. El aceite es rico en grasas poliinsaturadas, particularmente un ácido graso omega-6 llamado ácido gamma-linolénico (AGL). Las personas generalmente lo toman en cápsulas de gel blando por vía oral, generalmente estandarizado para contener un cierto porcentaje de AGL.
explanation_es.how_it_works_line: Proporciona bloques de construcción para moléculas de señalización antiinflamatorias en el cuerpo.
explanation_es.how_it_works: Cuando consume aceite de onagra, su cuerpo convierte el ácido gamma-linolénico (AGL) que contiene en otras moléculas de señalización —mensajeros químicos— llamadas metabolitos. Algunos de estos metabolitos pueden amortiguar las respuestas inflamatorias en el sistema inmunológico. La teoría es que al cambiar el equilibrio de estas señales inflamatorias, el aceite podría aliviar condiciones impulsadas por la inflamación, como los sofocos durante la menopausia o las condiciones inflamatorias de la piel. Sin embargo, la cadena exacta de eventos en humanos no está completamente mapeada; la mayoría de esta comprensión proviene de estudios celulares y en animales.
explanation_es.safety_line: Se han reportado efectos secundarios leves y reversibles en ensayos; muchas interacciones y poblaciones permanecen sin prueba.
explanation_es.safety_detail: Los ensayos clínicos recuperados reportan tolerabilidad generalmente buena, siendo los síntomas gastrointestinales leves (náuseas, hinchazón, indigestión) los efectos adversos más comunes. No emergieron señales de seguridad grave en los estudios mostrados, pero la mayoría de los ensayos fueron cortos (semanas a pocos meses) e incluyeron poblaciones relativamente limitadas (principalmente mujeres posmenopáusicas o pacientes con dermatitis atópica).
safety_bullets: Interacciones con medicamentos sin probar — el aceite de onagra teóricamente puede interactuar con anticoagulantes y fármacos antiplaquetarios; no se ha estudiado adecuadamente en humanos.
Embarazo y lactancia: no incluidos en los ensayos recuperados; la seguridad en estas poblaciones es desconocida.
Enfermedad renal o hepática: no representadas en las poblaciones de ensayos proporcionadas; los efectos en estos grupos no han sido verificados.
Dosis altas durante duraciones muy prolongadas: los ensayos recuperados son a corto plazo; la seguridad acumulativa no está establecida.
explanation_es.chem_meaning: El aceite de onagra es una mezcla de grasas, principalmente grasas poliinsaturadas omega-6. Esto significa que las moléculas son fluidas a la temperatura corporal y pueden disolverse en tejidos grasos, permitiendo que se absorban del intestino y se incorporen en las membranas celulares. El AGL dentro de él es relativamente voluminoso en comparación con grasas más simples, por lo que tarda más en absorberse y se convierte fácilmente por el cuerpo en otros compuestos.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Nueve ensayos clínicos y metanálisis, totalizando aproximadamente 1,596 participantes en el análisis agrupado más grande (2025), evaluaron el aceite de onagra para sofocos, sudores nocturnos y síntomas del estado de ánimo en mujeres posmenopáusicas. El análisis agrupado encontró una pequeña reducción en las puntuaciones de síntomas (diferencia media −2,13 puntos), pero el intervalo de confianza incluyó cero (−4,26 a 0,0), lo que significa que el efecto verdadero podría ser negligible. Los ensayos clínicos individuales de 2020–2023 reportaron resultados mixtos: algunos mostraron mejoras modestas en sofocos y síntomas psicológicos, otros mostraron poca diferencia respecto al placebo.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Existen múltiples estudios clínicos, pero el efecto agrupado cruza cero e los ensayos individuales muestran inconsistencia. Siete estudios primarios y dos metanálisis constituyen una base de evidencia moderada, pero la señal no está claramente separada del azar, por lo que la calificación permanece Moderada en lugar de Fuerte.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Tres ensayos clínicos (2020, 2022, 1989) y dos estudios en animales examinaron el efecto del aceite de onagra en los niveles de colesterol en sangre y perfiles de lípidos. Un metanálisis de 2020 agrupó resultados de ensayos controlados aleatorizados y encontró algún efecto en medidas de lípidos, aunque los tamaños de muestra en ensayos individuales fueron pequeños (el más grande verificado fue n=926 en el metanálisis mismo; los ensayos clínicos individuales citados fueron n=25 y tenían datos incompletos). Los estudios en animales (1998, 2022) mostraron reducciones en la coagulación vascular y acumulación de lípidos en conejos hiperliperémicos, pero los resultados en humanos siguen siendo modestos e inconsistentes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: La evidencia en humanos existe pero se basa principalmente en un único metanálisis sin replicación independiente de su conclusión. Los modelos en animales son de apoyo, pero la señal en humanos no es lo suficientemente grande o consistente para una calificación más alta. Moderada refleja datos en humanos alentadores pero no definitivos.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Cinco ensayos clínicos y un estudio en animales abordaron condiciones de la piel, principalmente dermatitis atópica y eczema. Un metanálisis de 2013 sobre aceite de onagra oral y aceite de borraja para eczema (n=1,596) encontró un efecto agrupado (diferencia media −2,22), pero como los síntomas menopaúsicos, el intervalo de confianza fue amplio (−10,48 a 6,04) y cruzó cero. Los ensayos individuales de 1996, 2018 y 2022 sobre dermatitis atópica y asma mostraron resultados variables. Un estudio en animales (2010) encontró que el aceite de onagra saponificado redujo la pigmentación de la piel y el daño inducido por rayos UV en células de melanoma.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Existen múltiples ensayos clínicos aleatorizados en humanos, pero el efecto agrupado es pequeño e impreciso, cruzando cero. No hay replicación independiente de la conclusión del metanálisis presente en los registros. Los datos en animales son de apoyo pero no mejoran la evidencia en humanos. Moderada refleja prueba genuina en humanos pero señales modestas e inconsistentes.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Solo un ensayo clínico aleatorizado en humanos (2018, n=80) y un estudio en animales (2014) fueron recuperados para la salud articular y la artritis. Notablemente, el ensayo clínico humano fue titulado 'Evening primrose oil and labour, is it effective?' —un contexto periparto, no una población clásica de artritis. El estudio en animales mostró que el aceite de onagra y el fármaco celecoxib juntos inhibieron la inflamación patológica y el estrés oxidativo en un modelo inflamatorio, pero los datos en humanos sobre enfermedad articular son mínimos.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Solo un pequeño ensayo clínico humano en una población diferente (periparto, no enfermedad articular establecida) y un estudio en animales de apoyo hacen que esto sea Emergente. No se puede juzgar la consistencia a partir de un único estudio clínico. La señal es preliminar y sin probar en una población dedicada de artritis.

explanation_es.evidence_base: El aceite de onagra ha sido estudiado principalmente en humanos, con la mayoría de la evidencia proveniente de mujeres posmenopáusicas y pacientes con dermatitis atópica. El cuerpo del trabajo está dominado por ensayos controlados aleatorizados y revisiones sistemáticas publicadas entre 1989 y 2025, con metanálisis recientes (2013, 2020, 2025) sintetizando datos antiguos y nuevos. Existen estudios en animales de apoyo pero son menos comunes. La evidencia es moderada en volumen (9–15 ensayos clínicos por resultado) pero inconsistente en el tamaño del efecto y la dirección, y la mayoría de los ensayos son a corto plazo (semanas a pocos meses).
explanation_es.open_questions: Los registros muestran que la mayoría de ensayos clínicos incluyen mujeres posmenopáusicas o personas con inflamación de la piel; los adultos más jóvenes, hombres y otras poblaciones permanecen en gran medida sin probar. No está claro si los efectos persisten más allá de unos pocos meses, ya que la mayoría de los ensayos recuperados son de corta duración. Los resultados menopaúsicos y de piel muestran resultados conflictivos incluso dentro de metanálisis, sugiriendo que el tamaño del efecto puede depender de la dosis, formulación (% de AGL estandarizado, aceite total), duración o factores de los pacientes no medidos — pero los resúmenes proporcionados no contienen el detalle necesario para resolver esto. Solo un ensayo abordó explícitamente articulaciones/artritis, haciendo que ese resultado sea altamente preliminar en los registros dados.

appraisal_es.headline: La base de evidencia se apoya fuertemente en RCTs pequeños, mayormente recientes, con resultados y poblaciones heterogéneos (eccema, síntomas menopáusicos, mastalgía, trabajo de parto); ningún resultado ha replicado hallazgos consistentes e independientes entre ensayos, y las estimaciones agrupadas para síntomas menopáusicos y resultados de piel incluyen cero o cruzan cero.

concerns.issue: Las estimaciones agrupadas abarcan o cruzan cero
concerns.detail: Para síntomas menopáusicos, el efecto agrupado es diferencia_media -2.13 [-4.26 a 0.0], lo que significa que el intervalo de confianza toca cero y el límite inferior es clínicamente negligible. Para piel/apariencia, la estimación agrupada es -2.22 [-10.48 a 6.04], que es extremadamente amplia e incluye beneficio sustancial, daño y ningún efecto. Estos intervalos de confianza no excluyen la hipótesis nula, lo que socava la confianza en cualquier magnitud de efecto.

concerns.issue: Un único metanálisis controla dos resultados sin replicación independiente
concerns.detail: Ambos resultados de colesterol y piel/apariencia se basan principalmente en un único metanálisis de 2020 (n=926 para lípidos, n=1596 para piel). El motor explícitamente señala que 'su conclusión no está replicada o verificada de forma independiente.' Si ese metanálisis contiene errores metodológicos, sesgo no medido o sesgo de publicación, la calificación completa para ambos resultados sería cuestionable. Ninguna revisión sistemática o metanálisis separado confirma estos hallazgos.

concerns.issue: El resultado de síntomas menopáusicos confunde múltiples poblaciones y diseños distintos
concerns.detail: De los 7 RCTs primarios para síntomas menopáusicos, uno (2018, n=80) se titula 'Evening primrose oil and labour'—abordando resultados del trabajo de parto, no síntomas menopáusicos. Otro (2002, n no reportado) aborda mastalgía. Un RCT de 2023 compara aceite de hinojo *y* aceite de onagra, lo que hace que la contribución individual sea poco clara. La heterogeneidad en poblaciones de pacientes (mujeres posmenopáusicas, trabajo de parto, mastalgía) e intervenciones (algunas combinadas con otros agentes) plantea preguntas sobre si estos ensayos miden el mismo constructo.

concerns.issue: La mayoría de los ensayos primarios son muy pequeños con tamaños de muestra no reportados
concerns.detail: Para síntomas menopáusicos: 7 de 9 estudios reportan n, pero solo 5 se muestran; 4 estudios no reportan tamaño de muestra en los registros. Para piel/apariencia: 3 de 6 estudios reportan n, y dos de esos son n=25 cada uno. Para colesterol: 2 de 5 estudios reportan n; 3 estudios no muestran tamaño de muestra en estos registros. Los ensayos pequeños son propensos a error aleatorio e informe selectivo; los tamaños de muestra no reportados sugieren posible sesgo de selección en qué estudios fueron recuperados o extraídos.

concerns.issue: Ningún resultado tiene replicación consistente entre ensayos humanos independientes
concerns.detail: Síntomas menopáusicos: 7 RCTs recuperados, pero solo 5 de 9 estudios reportan n; sin información sobre si los resultados individuales del ensayo concuerdan. Colesterol: solo 2 RCTs humanos reportados (n=25 y n no mostrado en ensayo de 1989); no se comparan narrativamente. Piel: 4 RCTs humanos, pero sin discusión sobre concordancia o discordancia entre ellos. El motor señala para articulaciones/artritis: 'la consistencia no puede ser evaluada entre evidencia humana independiente.' Este patrón sugiere que los ensayos pueden mostrar resultados variables que están oscurecidos por heterogeneidad o agrupamiento selectivo.

concerns.issue: El resultado de colesterol carece de estimación de efecto agrupado extractable
concerns.detail: Los registros establecen 'efecto agrupado: ninguno extractable' para el resultado de colesterol/lípidos, a pesar de que existe un metanálisis de 2020. Esto indica que los resúmenes disponibles no contienen la estimación metaanalítica (estimación puntual, IC o heterogeneidad). Los lectores no pueden verificar si el resultado agrupado respalda la calificación 'Moderada' o si la heterogeneidad fue alta. La calificación por lo tanto no es transparente.

concerns.issue: Agrupamiento de publicación reciente sin ensayos confirmatorios más antiguos
concerns.detail: Resultado de síntomas menopáusicos: 5 de 7 RCTs son de 2020–2025 (80% recientes); solo ensayos de 1996 y 2002 son anteriores a 2020. Piel: 4 de 5 ensayos humanos son 2018–2022. Este agrupamiento reciente sin evidencia confirmadora independiente más antigua plantea la posibilidad de que los ensayos más nuevos detectaran una señal en literatura más antigua y pequeña y luego la replicaran selectivamente, o que el aumento de interés condujo a sesgo de informe de resultados.

appraisal_es.mechanism_check: El aceite de onagra contiene ácido gamma-linolénico (GLA), un ácido graso poliinsaturado omega-6 que puede convertirse a DGLA y eicosanoides posteriores, que tienen propiedades antiinflamatorias in vitro y en modelos animales. El salto de la bioquímica antiinflamatoria al beneficio clínico en síntomas menopáusicos (vasomotores, psicológicos), reducción de colesterol o eccema es plausible pero indirecto: ningún estudio recuperado mide si el GLA oral logra de manera confiable concentraciones plasmáticas o tisulares suficientes para cambiar el metabolismo de eicosanoides en humanos, ni los ensayos clínicos demuestran el mecanismo propuesto en sus participantes. El mecanismo es conceptualmente sólido pero el vínculo entre el objetivo bioquímico y los resultados clínicos medidos no está validado empíricamente en estos ensayos.
appraisal_es.strongest_counterargument: Un escéptico señalaría que la estimación agrupada de síntomas menopáusicos incluye cero (IC cruza 0.0), sugiriendo ningún beneficio detectable sobre placebo; el IC del resultado de piel es enorme e incluye daño sustancial (-10.48) y beneficio (6.04), indicando que el efecto no se distingue claramente del ruido; y el resultado de colesterol carece de una estimación agrupada reportable en absoluto. El hecho de que el único metanálisis de 2020 controle tanto lípidos como piel, sin replicación independiente, significa que si ese metanálisis sobrestimó el tamaño del efecto (debido a sesgo de publicación, inclusión selectiva o sesgo de informe de resultados), toda la calificación moderada se colapsa. En los tres resultados principales, ningún resultado muestra una estimación agrupada que claramente excluya cero con intervalos de confianza estrechos—el sello distintivo de una base de evidencia de nivel moderado sólido sería uno o más hallazgos positivos robustos.
appraisal_es.what_would_change_the_picture: La replicación independiente del metanálisis de 2020 sobre lípidos y piel por un equipo separado usando protocolo pre-registrado prueba si los hallazgos son robustos. Para síntomas menopáusicos, un RCT grande (n ≥ 300 por rama), homogéneo, adecuadamente potenciado con resultado primario pre-registrado, evaluación de resultado cegada y protocolo publicado esclarecería si el efecto verdadero es nulo, pequeño o significativo; la incertidumbre de la estimación agrupada actual (cruzando cero) no lo resuelve. Un estudio mecanístico midiendo GLA/DGLA plasmáticos y metabolitos de eicosanoides en orina junto a resultados clínicos validaría la afirmación de plausibilidad biológica.
